messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi is a 47-year-old park ranger who lives alone in a small cabin on the outskirts of a national forest in the American South. He was born in Ghana and came to the United States in his twenties, but for the past several years he has worked in a vast, wooded preserve. The trauma that shattered his life occurred six years ago, during a visit to his home village during a period of civil conflict. He was caught in a militia attack that swept through his family’s compound. He survived by hiding in a dry brush thicket as flames consumed the structures around him, listening to the screams of neighbors and the crackle of fire. He emerged to find bodies and rubble, including his cousin’s body near the compound gate. He has not returned to Ghana since.

The memory of the fire is seared into Kofi’s senses. Now, in his daily work as a ranger, he is surrounded by the very landscape that echoes that day—the dry brush, the smell of pine, the sight of smoke from a distant campfire. Every time he patrols a wooded trail and the wind shifts, carrying the scent of burning wood, his chest tightens and his mind floods with images of flames. These triggers have become unbearable. He has begun to avoid entire sections of the park, taking longer routes that keep him far from areas where visitors might build fires. When a supervisor criticized him last month for taking an inefficient patrol path, Kofi felt a surge of panic that made no sense to him—the tone of correction felt like a condemnation, a reminder that he had failed to protect others. That evening, he drank heavily, a habit that has grown from a single beer after work to a bottle of whiskey most nights.

The guilt sits inside him like a stone. He believes he should have done more, that his survival was a kind of betrayal. When he sees a fire, or even hears a raised voice, the thought returns: *You are not the one who should be here.* This appraisal feeds into a constant low-level vigilance. He cannot relax, even in his own locked cabin. He lies awake at night, listening for sounds that are not there, his mind racing with imagined threats. When a ranger meeting runs long, he becomes convinced something terrible is happening—a fire, an attack—and he has to check his phone repeatedly. He has come to believe that any delay or criticism is a sign of impending danger, and this hypervigilance only deepens his isolation. He stopped answering calls from his sister in Accra, because hearing her voice made the guilt unbearable—she would ask about the village, and he could not speak of it.

Kofi’s isolation is almost total. He has not seen a friend in over a year. He avoids any reminder of military or police presence, which means he has stopped visiting the ranger station on days when the county sheriff’s deputies are there. He once walked out of a grocery store because a customer wore a camouflage jacket. This avoidance, in turn, strengthens his belief that he is fundamentally different from others, that he is set apart by what he did—or did not do. He has told no one the full story of that day. The more he isolates, the more the triggers multiply: a flicker of sunlight through leaves becomes the flash of fire; a distant shout becomes a warning. Each time, the threat feels real, and each time, he reaches for the bottle or retreats further into the woods.

He has come to therapy only because his employer mandated a fitness-for-duty evaluation after a hiker reported him for appearing disoriented and agitated near a controlled burn site. Kofi is afraid that he will lose his job, the only thing that still gives his life structure. But what frightens him most is the thought of being forced to talk about what happened, because he is certain that if he speaks the words aloud, the guilt will finally crush him.
